summary_plain: This investigation burns gaseous hydrocarbon flames inside a combustion chamber on the International Space Station to study how electric fields influence flame behavior in microgravity. By applying voltage, researchers observe changes in flame stability, soot, and combustion dynamics. Understanding these electric-field effects helps advance combustion science and technology.
summary_expert: Conducted as a flight investigation using the ACME hardware in the CIR on the International Space Station, ACME E-FIELD Flames investigated the effects of electric fields on laminar diffusion flames. The tested gas fuels included 100% C2H4, 100% CH4, 30% C2H4, and 40% CH4. The variables that changed between tests included the fuel type, mesh polarity, power supply, and co-flow burner position. Recorded outcomes across test runs included various flame ignition counts per test sequence, such as 10 flames ignited in 6 tests, 11 flames ignited in 6 tests, 13 flames ignited in 4 tests, 8 flames ignited in 2 tests, 15 flames ignited in 1 test, 12 flames ignited in 1 test, and 9 flames ignited in 1 test.

key_findings.text: The fuels and sample materials tested in ACME E-FIELD Flames were 100% C2H4, 100% CH4, 30% C2H4, and 40% CH4 gas fuels.

Recorded test outcomes in ACME E-FIELD Flames included test runs where 10 flames ignited in 6 tests, 11 flames ignited in 6 tests, 13 flames ignited in 4 tests, 8 flames ignited in 2 tests, 15 flames ignited in 1 test, 12 flames ignited in 1 test, and 9 flames ignited in 1 test.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 40 Follow-On Experiments We hope to have a third round of testing so that we can concentrate on flames in the coflow burner configuration that we found to be the more useful and symmetric than those with the jet burner.
